title: EvA: Evolutionary Attacks on Graphs
one_liner: Evolutionary algorithms beat gradient-based attacks because they search the discrete graph-flip space directly, avoiding the trick of pretending the problem is smooth when it is not.
lead: Graph neural networks (the AI models that reason about networks) can be broken by an attacker who flips connections between nodes. Old attacks use math (gradients) to guess which edge-flip will hurt the network most, but this math assumes the problem is smooth. In reality, a single edge flip might help even when math says it should not, because the network's reasoning changes unpredictably. EvA instead tries many different edge-flips directly, keeping the ones that actually work, without needing the math shortcut.

problem.h2: Why old attacks miss the true best flip
paras: A graph neural network reads a network — nodes are data points, edges are connections. An attacker wants to wreck the network's accuracy by flipping a few edges (add or remove them). Old attacks use calculus: they compute the gradient (which direction to nudge) and guess which edge-flip would shrink the error the most. But edge-flips are not smooth. Sometimes flipping an edge that math recommends actually hurts accuracy, because the network's reasoning changes in unexpected ways. The problem of finding the best flips has peaks and valleys that are disconnected from each other — the math shortcut does not work.

Old attacks dodge this by pretending the problem is smooth: instead of flipping edges (a discrete yes/no choice), they nudge edge-strength weights fractionally, then round at the end. This shortcut moves the answer far from real flips. It also requires the attack goal to be smooth (have a gradient). If your attack goal is strange (like fooling a verification (math that proves the network stays correct within a certain region) checker that does not use gradients), the old methods are stuck.

callout.html: Gradient math assumes smooth problems. Real edge-flips create peaks and valleys that the math overlooks.

steps.text: Start with random edge-flip candidates (different sets of edges to flip).
Run the network on the flipped graph, measure how much accuracy drops. No gradients required.
Select the flip-candidates that lowered accuracy the most.
Randomly tweak the top candidates (flip different edges) to explore nearby regions.
Loop until the attack finds the best possible flips within the budget.

paras: The paper changes which edge-flips the attack explores. Old methods search the relaxed continuous space and round; EvA searches the actual discrete space of real edge-flips directly. This is not a speed hack — it is a correctness shift. By abandoning the 'smooth it out' trick, EvA can find flips that gradients overlook, and it can handle objectives that have no gradient at all (like verification (math that proves the network stays correct within a certain region)).

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: How much does each edge flip matter
hidden.name: Edge importance (from direct evaluation)
paras: Old methods rank edges by their gradient: which edge-flip would math suggest shrinks the error? This works if the error surface is smooth, but it fails when reality has disconnected peaks and valleys. EvA instead measures importance directly: it flips an edge and sees what actually happens to the network's accuracy. The true importance is revealed only by running the network and measuring the real damage.

The paper uses this direct importance to decide which edges to flip in each generation. To keep memory low, the algorithm stores only the flipped edges themselves, not the entire graph, so it uses as much memory as the number of flips, not the number of connections. This lets it scale to large networks without running out of space.

heat.caption: Darker edge means that flip lowers accuracy more. No gradient math needed.

reads.html: EvA discovers which edges matter by trying to flip them and watching what happens.
The fitness function is the direct loss L evaluated on the perturbed graph, not a differentiable proxy.

mechanism.h2: Why evolutionary search finds better attacks than gradient tricks
paras: The error surface for graph edge-flips has peaks and valleys that do not connect smoothly. A gradient-based method assumes it is smooth and tries to roll downhill. In reality, flipping one edge might look good (lower error) but the network adapts in unexpected ways — the answer changes when you flip the next edge. Evolutionary algorithms do not assume smoothness. They explore many different flip-sets in parallel, score each one by running the real network, and keep only the ones that actually lower accuracy.

This parallel exploration works better because when the gradient method guesses 'flip this edge' and that guess is wrong in reality, the evolutionary method has already tried dozens of other edges and found ones that work. Each candidate is scored by running the actual network on actual flipped graphs, not by guessing from smooth math. For unusual attack goals (like fooling a verification (math that proves the network stays correct within a certain region) checker), there is often no gradient information at all, so the gradient method fails completely. The evolutionary method still works: it scores each flip-set and keeps improving.

The paper adds two tricks so the search can handle large graphs. First, sparse representation stores only the flipped edges, not the entire graph. This saves memory because the algorithm remembers just which edges to flip, so memory stays proportional to flip-budget, not graph-size — for a graph with 1000 nodes but only 10 allowed flips, the algorithm uses as much memory as 10 flips, not 1000 nodes, so it works on massive graphs that would exhaust memory otherwise. Second, divide-and-conquer splits the graph into two pieces, attacks each piece separately, then combines the results. Splitting reduces the exploration space: attacking a 100-node graph directly explores millions of possible flip combinations, but splitting into two 50-node pieces requires far fewer combinations to evaluate, so the search completes sooner.

stages.s: Graph and attack budget (how many edges to flip)
Run network on each; measure true accuracy drop
Keep best candidates; mutate and breed new ones
Repeat until converged or budget spent

math.h2: The attack objective in plain form
math.words: The attacker wants to find the set of edge-flips that maximize the loss (damage) on the network, subject to a budget constraint on how many flips are allowed.
math.equation: best_flips = arg max L(network(graph with flips), target) where number of flips <= budget
symbols: the set of edges to add or remove
the loss function measuring how wrong the network's predictions are
the network's output after the flips are applied
the true labels we want to trick the network about
the maximum number of edge-flips allowed

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the network is 100% accurate on a graph with 10 nodes and 15 edges.
Candidate 1: Flip edges 2, 5, 9 -> accuracy drops to 70% -> fitness = 30 (loss increase).
Candidate 2: Flip edges 1, 3, 4 -> accuracy drops to 45% -> fitness = 55.
Candidate 2 is kept; its edges are mutated (try flipping 1, 3, 7 instead) in the next generation.
After many generations, the attack finds a 3-edge flip that drops accuracy to 20%, fitness = 80.

math.note: The evolutionary algorithm never needs to compute gradients; it only needs to observe which flip-sets cause the largest accuracy drop.

bars.h2: Old attack vs EvA on real networks

charts.title: Gradient-based attack (PRBCD)
charts.note: Gradient method smooths the problem to make math work, then rounds the answer. This moves the solution away from real edge-flips.

charts.title: EvA (evolutionary search)
charts.note: EvA tries real edge-flips and scores them by running the network. It finds combinations that the smoothed version missed.

items.html: If the attacker is allowed to flip only 1 or 2 edges on a large graph, evolutionary search may not explore enough variants to find the critical edges. Gradients are slightly better here because they at least guess which edges matter.

items.b: Fitness function has no clear signal.
items.html: Evolutionary search needs a fitness function that distinguishes good flips from bad ones. If an attack objective is ambiguous (e.g., 'break the network a little bit'), the algorithm cannot tell which candidates to keep.

EvA evaluates many flip-candidates per generation, each requiring a forward pass through the network. When the attack budget is very small (1-2 flips) and the network is tiny, gradient methods are faster because they need only one gradient computation. EvA requires many forward passes to explore the flip-space.

When the attack objective is clear, the budget is reasonable (at least 5-10 flips), and the network is large enough to matter, EvA outperforms gradient methods by discovering flips that the smooth-space approximation missed.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small graph neural network (e.g., a 50-node citation network like Citeseer or Cora). Train it on 80% of nodes. Then run both an old gradient-based attack and EvA, each with a budget of 5 edge-flips. Measure the accuracy drop on the remaining 20% of nodes.
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy drop = original accuracy - accuracy after attack
demo.closing: EvA should achieve a larger accuracy drop with the same number of flips, because it discovered flips that the gradient method's smooth-space trick overlooked.
